# Scalar NA classes and class clusters

robjc represents a missing Scalar with an NA subclass rather than a state of the ordinary value class.
Users pass values to the ordinary class, but `$new(NA)` returns an instance of the NA subclass.
This difference between the class called and the class returned is a class cluster.
This note (06) explains the relevant paths in `RSScalarClass()` and `RSScalar$initialize()`.
See [note 02](tech_02_new_initialize.Rmd) for why `$new()` uses the result of initialization.

## `RSScalarClass()` creates two classes

`RSScalarClass()` creates an ordinary class from the specified parent Scalar, followed by an NA subclass of that ordinary class.
For a name starting with `RS`, this produces a pair such as `RSNumber` and `RSNANumber`.
The NA subclass has `isNAClass = TRUE`, while the ordinary class has `isNAClass = FALSE`.
They have separate `isa` environments, but an NA instance is also an instance of the ordinary class's lineage.

```{r}
library(robjc)

stopifnot(identical(RSNumber$na$class(), RSNANumber))
stopifnot(identical(RSNANumber$robjc_isa$super, RSNumber))
stopifnot(!RSNumber$isNAClass)
stopifnot(RSNANumber$isNAClass)
stopifnot(RSNumber$na$isKindOf(RSNumber))
```

Once it has created the NA subclass, the factory creates one instance with the supplied `na_value`.
It stores that instance in the NA subclass's `$instance` and `robjc_isa$slot`, and in the ordinary class's `$na` and `robjc_isa$slot`.
The default NA instance is thus reachable from either class.

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(RSNumber$na, RSNumber$robjc_isa$slot))
stopifnot(identical(RSNumber$na, RSNANumber$instance))
stopifnot(identical(RSNANumber$instance, RSNANumber$robjc_isa$slot))
```

## Switch classes through the return value of `initialize()`

`$new(value)` first allocates an instance of the ordinary class and calls `initialize(value)`.
The type-specific initializer validates its input and passes it to `super$initialize(value)`.
When `RSScalar$initialize()` receives a valid NA and the current class is not the NA subclass, it returns the NA instance from `isa$slot`.
Because robjc's `$new()` returns that value, the caller receives the NA subclass instance instead of the instance initially allocated.

```text
RSNumber$new(NA_real_)
  → allocate an RSNumber instance
  → RSNumber$initialize() validates the type
  → RSScalar$initialize() returns RSNumber$robjc_isa$slot
  → RSNumber$new() returns the shared RSNANumber instance
```

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(RSNumber$new(NA_real_), RSNumber$na))
stopifnot(RSNumber$new(1L)$isMemberOf(RSNumber))
stopifnot(!RSNumber$new(1L)$isMemberOf(RSNANumber))
```

The type-specific `initialize()` must propagate the result of `super$initialize(value)` all the way out.
Returning `invisible(self)` unconditionally after receiving an NA instance would discard the class switch.
For example, `RSNumber$initialize()` validates the type and leaves `super$initialize(val)` as its final expression.
`RSDateTime$initialize()` normalizes the POSIX value and explicitly returns the parent's result if it differs from `self`.

## Initializing the NA subclass itself

Before initializing the newly created NA subclass with `na_value`, the factory sets its `isNAClass` to `TRUE`.
For an NA subclass, `RSScalar$initialize()` rejects non-NA values and stores a valid NA in the private `.val`.
It does not switch to another instance, because the current instance already has the correct class.

With the default `na_singleton = TRUE`, the factory replaces the NA subclass's `$new()` with an error after creating its shared instance.
Use the ordinary class's `$na` or `$new(NA)` to obtain that shared NA.
See [note 02](tech_02_new_initialize.Rmd) for the rules on direct construction and how `RSNull$new()` differs.

```{r}
stopifnot(inherits(tryCatch(RSNANumber$new(NA_real_), error = identity), "error"))
stopifnot(identical(RSNumber$new(NA_real_), RSNumber$na))
```

## Distinguish NA from NaN

`RSScalar$initialize()` checks `is.nan(value)` as well as `is.na(value)`.
Although R also considers `is.na(NaN)` true, robjc keeps `NaN` as an ordinary Scalar value.
Each class validates input type and length before switching to a shared NA.

```{r}
nan <- RSNumber$new(NaN)
stopifnot(nan$isMemberOf(RSNumber))
stopifnot(!nan$isMemberOf(RSNANumber))
stopifnot(is.nan(nan$value()))
```

## `RSFactor` does not use one shared NA for every input

A missing factor can retain levels and ordering information.
One shared instance cannot hold different `levels()` and `is.ordered()` settings for each input.
`RSFactor` therefore specifies `na_singleton = FALSE`, allowing direct construction of its NA subclass, `RSNAFactor`.
When `RSFactor$new()` receives a missing factor, it creates and returns a new `RSNAFactor`.
`RSFactor$na` remains the default NA instance created by the factory.

```{r}
low_high <- factor(NA_character_, levels = c("low", "high"), ordered = TRUE)
small_large <- factor(NA_character_, levels = c("small", "large"))
first <- RSFactor$new(low_high)
second <- RSFactor$new(small_large)

stopifnot(first$isMemberOf(RSNAFactor))
stopifnot(second$isMemberOf(RSNAFactor))
stopifnot(!identical(first, second))
stopifnot(!identical(first, RSFactor$na))
stopifnot(identical(first$asFactor(), low_high))
stopifnot(identical(second$asFactor(), small_large))
```

## Raw values without an NA subclass

Base R's `raw` type has no NA value.
`RSRaw` therefore inherits directly from `RSObject`, is declared with `RSObjectClass()`, and has no NA subclass.
`RSNull` is a separate Singleton representing R's `NULL`; its role differs from a Scalar NA class.

A class cluster selects a construction path that preserves type-specific information, in addition to representing missing values with a separate class.
To inspect the class returned, use `object$class()` or `isKindOf()` as well as the value's `is.na()`.
